justification_text:
My point estimates at each horizon reflect the trend I expect in the variable I was forecasting, based on the data I had at the time. For the 1-day horizon, the small change relative to the initial value suggests that the variable is fairly stable and subject to only minor, predictable fluctuations in the very short term. By the 1-week and 1-month horizons, I incorporated broader trends or expectations of gradual adjustments. For instance, the 1-week estimate of 344.5 reflects a modest upward drift, possibly driven by anticipated underlying drivers such as momentum, seasonal patterns, or external factors I factored in. The 1-month estimate of 348.2 represents a continuation of this trend, projecting that any gradual forces acting on the variable will likely accumulate over the longer period.

The widths of the confidence intervals (CIs) capture the uncertainty at each time frame. In the short term, fewer unknowns influence the outcome, so the 1-day CI is quite narrow. Over a week, uncertainty increases as more factors (like unexpected news, shifts in sentiment, or random noise) have time to come into play, widening the interval. By the 1-month horizon, the range of possible scenarios expands significantly, reflecting the cumulative uncertainty of compounding small changes, potential market corrections, or external shocks. The wide CI for 1 month also acknowledges that long-term forecasts are inherently more difficult due to the complex interplay of variables over time.

There are certainly risks and unforeseen events that could push the outcomes outside the stated confidence intervals. For instance, if this forecast pertains to financial markets, a major economic announcement, central bank decision, geopolitical event, or corporate earnings surprise could lead to abrupt changes far exceeding normal expectations. Similarly, in scenarios where external shocks—such as natural disasters, policy changes, or technological breakthroughs—play a role, the actual variable could deviate well beyond the bounds of the forecast intervals. My model likely assumes a normal level of randomness and typical variations, but these sharp or rare events could push the outcomes outside the expected range.
